title: How Italy Spawned the Western Far Right
gist: Michele Barbero reviews Jason Horowitz's memoir 'The Italian Job', which argues Italy has been a laboratory for the Western far right: Berlusconi set the template for Trump and mainstreamed the post-fascist right, culminating in Meloni's 2022 win, a pattern now spreading across Europe. Italy's fragmented system and strong judiciary may tame the far right in ways other countries with stronger executives cannot.

insights.claim: Jason Horowitz's memoir 'The Italian Job' argues that Italy, far from being politically marginal, has served as a laboratory for political trends that later spread across Europe and the United States, including the rise of the modern far right.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Italian political developments can serve as a leading indicator for populist shifts in larger Western economies.

insights.claim: Silvio Berlusconi served as a template for Donald Trump: a brand-name businessman with media access and charisma who exploited a weakened political mainstream and attacked legal cases as 'witch hunts'.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Pattern-matching Berlusconi's trajectory helps anticipate the policy and institutional behavior of Trump-style leaders.
insights.quote: “Berlusconi set the mold for Trump, the Italian original before the American knockoff,” Horowitz writes.
insights.locator: Berlusconi set the mold for Trump

insights.claim: Berlusconi resigned in 2011 amid an acute financial crisis that threatened to push the eurozone's third-largest economy into default.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: A reminder that Italian political crises have historically coincided with eurozone sovereign-debt stress.
insights.locator: A sizable share of the book

insights.claim: By repeatedly bringing the far right into coalition governments, Berlusconi broke the firewall around it and paved the way for Giorgia Meloni's 2022 election as prime minister.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Shows how center-right coalition choices can normalize far-right parties, a dynamic now playing out elsewhere in Europe.
insights.locator: On top of inspiring the future

insights.claim: Berlusconi correctly bet that including the post-fascist Italian Social Movement in government would moderate it, but failed to foresee his far-right partners eventually sidelining Forza Italia.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Mainstream parties that co-opt the far right risk being displaced by it, reshaping governing coalitions.

insights.claim: Giorgia Meloni became the first far-right head of government in western Europe since World War II, exactly a century after Mussolini's march on Rome.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Marks a historic normalization of far-right governance in a G7 economy.
insights.locator: After two more coalitions quickly rotated

insights.claim: Meloni has pursued a staunchly conservative agenda of curtailing abortion rights, banning surrogacy and strengthening police powers, but most Italians the reviewer speaks to do not see her as a threat to democratic freedoms.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Suggests far-right governance in Italy has been socially conservative but institutionally stable, limiting market-moving political risk.

insights.claim: Italy's far-right trend is being replicated across Europe: populist nationalists have backed or joined governments in Sweden and the Netherlands, Marine Le Pen leads France's presidential race, Reform U.K. tops polls, and the AfD has gained on Germany's Christian Democrats.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Rising populist odds in France, the U.K. and Germany raise European policy and fiscal uncertainty.

insights.claim: In 2018, Italy became a beacon for international right-wing populists such as Steve Bannon when League leader Matteo Salvini became interior minister in a coalition with the Five Star Movement.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Illustrates transnational networking among populist movements.
insights.quote: Italy was “the place to be for the most eager arsonists of the existing world order.”

insights.claim: Italy's fragmented political system and strong judiciary, designed after World War II for strong checks and balances, may restrain the far right in ways that countries with fewer constitutional ramparts cannot.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Institutional design matters for pricing the risk of far-right governments in different countries.
insights.locator: As to whether the far right

insights.claim: France concentrates far greater power in the executive than Italy, illustrated by Emmanuel Macron forcing through the 2023 pension reform without a legislative vote, which could matter if the far right wins there.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: A Le Pen presidency could wield stronger unilateral power than Meloni, raising French policy risk.

insights.claim: Poor job opportunities and low salaries are prompting large numbers of talented Italian graduates to emigrate.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Brain drain weighs on Italy's productivity and long-term growth potential.
insights.locator: The lack of good job opportunities

insights.claim: Italy's aging population is straining its welfare state and its family-based model of elder care.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Demographic pressure adds to Italy's long-term fiscal burden.
insights.locator: The lack of good job opportunities

insights.claim: Horowitz suggests Italians' insistence on following traditional recipes to the letter may reflect a broader cultural reluctance to embrace change and innovation.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Cultural resistance to change may help explain Italy's persistently slow productivity growth.

insights.claim: The reviewer argues Horowitz underrates the Five Star Movement's gradual shift from an anti-establishment movement to a more mainstream, moderate, left-leaning party.
insights.speaker: Michele Barbero
insights.so_what: Italy's opposition landscape is less radical than often portrayed.
